sm: The Franklin Board of Mayor and Aldermen opened its work session with roll call, and no citizen comments were offered on non-agenda items. Staff explained a contract with the state Comptroller for a new annual compliance attestation that the mayor must sign and file by January first. Staff then presented draft resolution 2026-104 setting budget goals for fiscal 2028. Foundational goals include a structurally balanced budget, compliance with reserve and debt policies, and on-time delivery of the ten-year capital program. Areas of emphasis include fiscal limits tied to sales tax reliance and possible state limits on property tax, attainable housing, workforce recruitment and retention, intergovernmental relations, and infrastructure delivery.

Staff finished the budget goals with infrastructure and service items. These included the transit, parking and pedestrian plans, intersection improvements, the South Clean Water Plant, biosolids and compost capacity, glass recycling, and efficient use of AI. A resolution is planned for the December meeting. In answer to a question, staff said the housing fund would only be explored in the coming year, not fully funded. Alderman Burger asked that cost savings, innovation and rewards for employee ideas be emphasized, and staff said efficiency is built into the budget process. Another member noted the budget has grown conservatively. Staff said the general fund grew about two percent last year and all funds about three percent.

Staff said the ten-year capital program is about 460 million dollars, with roughly seventy percent paid in cash and thirty percent by debt. The board then turned to biosolids storage sites. Assistant Water Director Taylor Hopkins explained that the city treats its biosolids to Class A exceptional quality, usable on farms and gardens. Demand is seasonal, and mixing with compost improves the product. Landfilling costs sixty-five dollars a ton for about six thousand tons a year, roughly 360,000 dollars. Three city-owned sites were identified, on Otter's Gate Way, at the water reclamation facility, and on Old Carter's Creek Pike. The Otter's Gate Way site is mostly in the floodplain, with about four usable acres.

Staff described the remaining sites. The water reclamation facility site is also largely in the floodplain, and it drew neighborhood concern years ago because of its closeness to Franklin High School and Chestnut Bend. The Old Carter's Creek Pike site is about two and a half acres, has all utilities, and sits close to the compost facility. It needs demolition of old tanks, a fence and a gate. Staff called it the most viable site the city owns. A user survey showed some interest in buying the blended material. Alderman Blanton noted that material would need hauling between the compost site and wherever the biosolids are stored. Staff agreed some trucking is unavoidable.

Alderman Burger asked about mileage to the compost site. Two residents then spoke against the Carter's Creek project. The Reverend Dr. James Green said his group did not want odor in the area. Eric Martin asked what neighbors would see, smell and experience in traffic. Hopkins said the material smells like dirt, and that about one dump truck a day would haul about twenty tons of biosolids. He said timing could be adjusted, and the site would have a small office and open storage buildings. A board member asked about setback and screening rules, which staff did not know. Another member said the issue got off on the wrong foot after news coverage.

Board members urged broad public meetings and formal site tours so residents can see the process. One said touring the new plant with homeowners association leaders eased complaints, since the odor they blamed did not come from the plant. Alderman Brown said stewardship of the city asset is separate from whether to support the Homeless Alliance. He still had questions about the alliance's exit strategy. Alderman Potts learned that a future water plant's solids would go to the existing biosolids facility, and that sales would work like the compost facility. Another member said he was hesitant to give or sell any of the three city properties to any organization. The board then moved on to the transit fund.

Chief Budget Performance Officer Michael Walters Young previewed an audit finding to go to the Budget and Finance Committee on December third. The transit fund overspent its budget in fiscal 2026. It had an original budget of 4.33 million dollars, amended to 4.73 million, against actual spending of 5.54 million, an overage of about 809,000 dollars, or 17.1 percent. Grant programs accounted for about 536,000 dollars. The city passes through county and WeGo vanpool money, and van purchases were not reflected in an amended budget. Transit operations ran over by about 340,000 dollars, including a facility relocation, 40,409 dollars in insurance, and nearly 200,000 dollars of unexpected costs. He took responsibility for the budget office and described new monthly budget reviews.

Young described more fixes. A first budget amendment of nearly a million dollars will come to committee on December third. Vanpool purchases had run 250,000 to 400,000 dollars a year but reached 1.1 million last year as vans aged out. The fund balance fell from about 800,000 to just over 500,000 dollars. Staff will decide whether to cut expenses or raise the city's 1.46 million dollar contribution. Other steps include more detailed accounts, February training for the transit authority board, vanpool budgets in its reports, and a contract review. Alderman Brown asked why vehicles were treated as operating costs. Staff said the vans are owned by the county or WeGo, so the city books them as pass-through expenses. The audit goes to the full board on December eighth.

Aldermen asked whether the vanpool will get a replacement schedule, and staff said what matters most is correct budgeting for money flowing through. Asked about unexplained miscellaneous costs of 42,387 dollars, staff said this scale of overage had not happened in twelve years. Staff expected no effect on the AAA bond rating, noting a past finding was fixed and the rating reaffirmed twice. Fund balance fell from 807,254 dollars to 584,249 dollars, a drop of 223,005 dollars. One alderman stressed the vanpool purchases were not city taxpayer dollars. He suggested better communication with the transit authority and possibly county involvement.

A transit authority representative said the vanpool money is federal and state, with no county dollars. He said the problems came from contract changes and from not knowing a budget amendment was needed. He credited new staff for catching the issues and said it will not happen again. The board then took up the Preserve at Sheridan development, a fifteen-lot project on 52 acres at South Berry's Chapel Road. Assistant City Administrator Walter Denton said its plan required a northbound left turn lane on Franklin Road. The estimate rose from 239,000 dollars to about 1.1 million, because the shoulder cannot carry through traffic. He offered four options, including keeping the requirement.

Denton listed the options. Option A keeps the requirement, B has the city share cost, C takes the developer's 239,000 dollars toward a future Franklin Road project, and D drops the requirement. Anything besides A requires amending the development plan through the board. Alderman Brown opposed adding costs, noting the development shrank to fifteen lots and only about five homes are expected soon. He favored collecting fees and holding them for Franklin Road. Others noted the turn lane is critical for morning northbound traffic. Alderman Blanton leaned toward options B or C. She noted a 25 to 30 million dollar Franklin Road widening is not funded in the ten-year plan.

Some members said they disliked going back through the Planning Commission. Developer David Blackburn explained that a milling and restriping plan was first costed. Core samples then showed the shoulder was only about eight inches of gravel and four layers of asphalt, and two feet of the existing road was built the same way. That raised the cost. He said his impact fees total about 900,000 dollars, with about 275,000 for roads. He said he would accept options C or D, and that he had also paid over 100,000 dollars for a culvert at Berry's Chapel. Engineer Brandon Baxter said the cost was out of balance for a fifteen-home development. Staff said the existing approved condition must be formally changed.

Staff said the development plan was resubmitted for the November thirtieth deadline, so changes could be folded in. Staff could not cite an exact precedent but said conditions sometimes change. Members questioned why the state would require a rebuild of a road it built, and raised the safety and traffic problems at the left turn. Several said they could not wait ten years for the Franklin Road widening. Some asked what threshold would justify revisiting conditions for other developers. One member said the public would object if the requirement were dropped.

Staff said there is no approved project or funding for a forty million dollar widening. The capital plan holds about 14 million dollars for spot improvements. Staff will ask the state for help but do not expect relief. Several aldermen, including Barnhill, Blanton and Potts, leaned toward option B, city cost sharing. Some suggested capping the city share, with figures around 750,000 to 850,000 dollars discussed. Alderman Potts favored an even fifty-fifty split of the 1.1 million. Others wanted staff to look for cheaper approaches.

Alderman Brown suggested coordinating with a state paving project coming in spring. The mayor summarized two versions of cost sharing. In one, the city fills the gap between 239,000 and 1.1 million dollars, about 860,000. In the other, a fifty-fifty split would cost the city about 550,000 and the developer about 311,000 dollars. Alderman Baggett asked about using spot-fix money. One member objected that both parties agreed to the plan and the city should not carry the added cost. The board then moved to the 2026 to 2035 capital investment plan financial model. Staff said this refresh shows limited capacity.

Young reported about 11 million dollars more has been spent on ongoing projects. Cash resources peaked near 100 million dollars in fiscal 2022 and have been declining. The model last year forecast 460 million dollars, seventy percent cash and thirty percent debt at 139.1 million. It now shows about 468 million over ten years, with debt unchanged and no new debt assumed. Road impact fee growth and retiring debt service boost outer years. The 3.4 cents of property tax set aside supports the Mac Hatcher Southeast match with the state, built on a fifty million dollar twenty-year bond. There are 26 approved projects totaling 458 million dollars. Only about 10 million dollars is unprogrammed, so a big Franklin Road upgrade is constrained.

Staff said they may bring back specific spot improvements for Franklin Road and weigh them against the larger concept discussed two weeks earlier. The mayor and city recorder Casey then described a new rule for applicant materials. Presentations, photographs and exhibits must be emailed to the city recorder by 4 p.m. the Thursday before a meeting. They will be posted electronically for the board and the public. Slides will not be pulled up unless the board asks. Aldermen worried about last-minute changes, printing costs and limits on applicants. Staff said late submissions can be accommodated, handouts remain allowed, and the process will stay flexible. A recess was called until ten after.
